name: Recruitment vs selection
purpose: What is the difference between attracting candidates and choosing among them – and why does the order matter?

parts.label: Job analysis
points: Job description and person specification
Defines the criteria for everything after

parts.label: Recruitment
points: Attracting the right pool of candidates
Good recruitment makes selection possible

parts.label: Selection
points: Applying techniques to identify the right candidates out of the pool
Techniques must be valid, reliable and practicable

parts.label: Induction
points: Integrating the new hire

apply: Start from the job description: highlight the key issues the job involves
Build the recruitment strategy (where and how to attract) and then the selection strategy (how to choose)
Justify each step with person–organisation fit, context and cost-effectiveness
pitfalls: Mixing the two: a job ad is recruitment, an assessment centre is selection
example: Inditex case: develop a recruitment AND a selection strategy for one of two positions in different countries.

name: Validity, reliability & practicability
purpose: How do I judge – and defend – a selection method?

parts.label: Validity
points: Does the method measure what predicts performance in THIS job?
Which aspect of the job description does it measure?

parts.label: Reliability
points: Consistent results across raters, candidates and time
Structured, standardized methods help

parts.label: Practicability
points: Cost, time, volume of applicants
Acceptance by candidates, legal constraints
→ cost-effectiveness

apply: For each method: name the criterion from the job description it measures (validity)
Explain how the methods work together to increase validity and reliability
Check repetitions: do two methods look at the same criterion? Is that necessary and cost-effective?
Check coverage: are all relevant requirements of the job description evaluated?
pitfalls: Listing methods without saying what each one measures
Forgetting practicability: an assessment centre for 5,000 store applicants is not workable

name: Designing a recruitment strategy
purpose: Which choices does a recruitment strategy have to balance?

parts.label: Informing vs attracting
points: Balance the organisation's and the candidate's needs
Realistic information vs selling the job

parts.label: Internal vs external
points: Consider internal recruitment: known performers, motivation, cheaper
External: new skills, larger pool

parts.label: Standard vs local
points: Same firm, different countries: labour market, channels, culture

parts.label: Broad vs targeted channels
points: Volume vs quality of applications
Cost per hire

apply: Position the case on each axis and justify with the job description and the context
Choose channels that reach the target pool (and diverse candidates)
pitfalls: More applications ≠ better hires: CIPD 2026 – 58 % saw more applications, only 33 % more suitable candidates

name: Recruitment in numbers (CIPD 2026)
origin: CIPD Resourcing and Talent Planning Report 2026
purpose: What does the evidence say about attraction methods, quality and cost of hiring?

parts.label: Volume ≠ quality
points: 58 % of employers saw more applications, only 33 % more suitable candidates
53 % had difficulties attracting candidates, mainly senior and skilled roles (18 % also for low-skilled)

parts.label: Most effective attraction methods
points: Own corporate website (40 %)
Generic job boards (35 %)
Internal advertising to existing talent pool (32 %)
Recruitment/search consultants (29 %)
Targeted campaigns on professional networks (28 %)
Employee referrals and organic content (24 % each)

parts.label: Median cost per hire
points: Senior managers/directors: £3,500 (2026)
Other employees: £2,000 (2026)
Costs include technology, advertising, agency fees, tests, onboarding

apply: Use the numbers to justify channel choice and cost-effectiveness in a recruitment recommendation
pitfalls: Quoting numbers without linking them to the case job
